items.c: Remember: diabetic macular edema on OCT shows multilocular intraretinal cysts in the inner and outer nuclear layers, and centre-involved disease is treated with anti-VEGF therapy.
items.a: Diabetic macular edema

items.c: Remember: large drusen (greater than 125 micrometres) with or without pigmentary change define intermediate AMD, and the AREDS2 supplement plus smoking cessation are the key modifiable measures.
items.a: Age-related macular degeneration (intermediate)

items.c: Remember: Late AMD on OCT = RPE elevation or atrophy plus outer retinal disruption in an older adult with drusen; geographic atrophy is the dry form and CNV is the wet form.
items.a: Age-related macular degeneration (late)

items.c: Remember: Diabetic macular edema is intraretinal cystic fluid on OCT in a diabetic patient, and central subfield thickness guides anti-VEGF treatment.
items.a: Diabetic macular edema

items.c: Remember: a dome-shaped sub-RPE elevation in an older patient with drusen points to late AMD (pigment epithelial detachment or neovascular change), not central serous chorioretinopathy.
items.a: Age-related macular degeneration (late)

items.c: Remember: Late AMD on OCT shows RPE elevation (pigment epithelial detachment), intraretinal or subretinal fluid and cysts, and subretinal fibrosis or atrophy; age over 50 with painless central vision loss and metamorphopsia is the classic presentation.
items.a: Age-related macular degeneration (late)

items.c: Remember: a hyperreflective inner retinal membrane with wrinkling and an intact outer retina on OCT is an epiretinal membrane, the commonest cause of macular pucker.
items.a: Epiretinal membrane

items.c: Remember: Epiretinal membrane on OCT appears as a hyperreflective inner surface band with retinal corrugation and preserved foveal architecture, and it is treated with vitrectomy and membrane peeling when vision is significantly affected.
items.a: Epiretinal membrane

items.c: Remember: epiretinal membrane shows a hyperreflective inner surface band with retinal wrinkling and an intact foveal pit, causing metamorphopsia with preserved or mildly reduced vision.
items.a: Epiretinal membrane

items.c: Remember: retinal vein occlusion with macular oedema shows diffuse intraretinal thickening with loss of the foveal depression on OCT, and always look for systemic hypertension, diabetes, and glaucoma as risk factors.
items.a: Retinal vein occlusion (KME)

items.c: Remember: in retinal vein occlusion, cystoid macular oedema is the commonest cause of central vision loss, and it is treated first-line with anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy.
items.a: Retinal vein occlusion (KME)

items.c: Remember: in late retinal vein occlusion the OCT shows chronic cystoid macular edema, disorganised inner retina and outer retinal atrophy, so think of venous occlusion when diffuse hemorrhages and tortuosity coexist with macular cysts.
items.a: Retinal vein occlusion (late)

items.c: Remember: diffuse haemorrhages in all four quadrants plus tortuous veins suggest CRVO, and cystic intraretinal spaces on OCT indicate CME, the main cause of visual loss in RVO.
items.a: Retinal vein occlusion (KME)

items.c: Remember: a full-thickness macular hole on OCT shows a full-thickness foveal defect with the edges separated, and vitreomacular traction is a key cause that is often treated with vitrectomy.
items.a: Vitreomacular interface disease (MH)

items.c: Remember: a full-thickness macular hole is a full-thickness foveal defect with a premacular cuff, and vitrectomy with ILM peeling is the standard treatment.
items.a: Vitreomacular interface disease (MH)

items.c: Remember: vitreomacular traction is an incomplete posterior vitreous detachment with a taut vitreous strand attached to the fovea, and it is the key precursor lesion to full-thickness macular hole.
items.a: Vitreomacular interface disease (VMT)

items.c: Remember: in glaucoma, the disc changes (rim thinning, notching, enlarged cup, vessel bayonetting) precede visual field loss, so a cup-to-disc ratio asymmetry above 0.2 between the eyes warrants full glaucoma work-up even with a normal IOP.
items.a: Glaucomatous disc

items.c: Remember: a deep, enlarged cup with focal rim notching and nasal vessel bayoneting in a patient with raised IOP points to glaucomatous optic neuropathy.
items.a: Glaucomatous disc

items.c: Remember: Glaucomatous optic neuropathy is a structural diagnosis; a large cup with thinned rim and nasal vessel displacement signals damage even when intraocular pressure is only borderline raised.
items.a: Glaucomatous disc

items.c: Remember: a large cup-to-disc ratio with rim thinning and vessel bayoneting in a patient with raised IOP or an arcuate field defect means glaucoma until proven otherwise.
items.a: Glaucomatous disc

items.c: Remember: glaucomatous optic neuropathy is recognised by increased cup-to-disc ratio, focal rim thinning or notching, and bayoneting of vessels; IOP lowering is the only proven treatment.
items.a: Glaucomatous disc

items.c: Remember: Normal retina with a clear disc, normal vessels and no microaneurysms or haemorrhages equals no diabetic retinopathy, so routine annual screening is sufficient.
items.a: No retinopathy

items.c: Remember: mild NPDR = microaneurysms only; the first clinical sign of diabetic retinopathy is the microaneurysm, and the moment haemorrhages beyond minimal number, cotton wool spots, or venous beading appear, the grade becomes moderate.
items.a: Mild non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR)

items.c: Remember: Moderate NPDR = microaneurysms plus dot-and-blot haemorrhages or hard exudates in more than one quadrant, but no severe NPDR or PDR features (4-2-1 rule for severe NPDR: haemorrhages in 4 quadrants, venous beading in 2, IRMA in 1).
items.a: Moderate non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR)

items.c: Remember: Moderate NPDR = more than microaneurysms only (haemorrhages, hard exudates, or cotton wool spots) but less than severe criteria; Severe NPDR needs 4-2-1 rule findings (haemorrhages in 4 quadrants, venous beading in 2 quadrants, or IRMA in 1 quadrant).
items.a: Moderate non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR)

items.c: Remember: Mild NPDR = microaneurysms only; Moderate NPDR = haemorrhages, microaneurysms, and/or exudates beyond mild but short of severe; Severe NPDR = 4-2-1 rule; PDR = neovascularisation.
items.a: Moderate non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR)

items.c: Remember: Moderate NPDR = more than microaneurysms only (haemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton-wool spots) but not meeting severe NPDR criteria; no neovascularisation.
items.a: Moderate non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR)

items.c: Remember: moderate NPDR = more than microaneurysms only, with dot/blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, or cotton wool spots in fewer than four quadrants, and no neovascularisation.
items.a: Moderate non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR)

items.c: Remember the 4-2-1 rule: haemorrhages and microaneurysms in 4 quadrants, venous beading in 2 or more quadrants, or IRMA in 1 quadrant defines severe NPDR, with about 50 percent risk of progression to PDR within 1 year.
items.a: Severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR)

items.c: Remember the 4-2-1 rule: severe NPDR = more than 20 hemorrhages in 4 quadrants, OR definite venous beading in 2 or more quadrants, OR prominent IRMA in 1 or more quadrant; any of these without neovascularisation makes it severe NPDR with about 50 percent one-year progression risk
items.a: Severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR)

items.c: Remember the 4-2-1 rule: haemorrhages in 4 quadrants, venous beading in 2 quadrants, or IRMA in 1 quadrant defines severe NPDR, with a high risk of progression to PDR within a year.
items.a: Severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR)

items.c: Remember: Proliferative means new vessels (NVD, NVE) or vitreous or preretinal haemorrhage; treat with panretinal photocoagulation or anti-VEGF.
items.a: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR)

items.c: Remember: new vessels on the disc (NVD) or elsewhere (NVE), or vitreous/preretinal haemorrhage, define PDR and mandate PRP or anti-VEGF.
items.a: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR)

items.c: Remember: any neovascularisation of the disc (NVD) or elsewhere (NVE) equals PDR, regardless of how few haemorrhages are present; the 4-2-1 rule identifies high-risk severe NPDR, which is one step from PDR.
items.a: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR)

items.c: Remember: at 28 weeks gestation, screening is mandatory, and a normal fundus with full posterior vascularisation indicates no ROP, but rescreening is still required because risk persists.
items.a: No retinopathy of prematurity (ROP)

items.c: Remember: laser scars with a demarcated avascular peripheral retina in a preterm infant indicate laser-treated ROP, and follow-up is essential because late recurrence and retinal detachment can still occur.
items.a: Laser-treated ROP

items.c: Remember: Stage 4 is partial detachment, Stage 5 is total funnel detachment; the funnel shape and disc displacement toward the lens define Stage 5 and signal a poor visual outcome.
items.a: Stage 5

items.c: Remember: in glaucoma, the cup enlarges and the neuroretinal rim thins, typically in the inferior and superior poles first (ISNT rule violated), and a vertical CDR above 0.6 or asymmetry greater than 0.2 is highly suspicious.
items.a: Optic disc cupping

items.c: Remember: a tilted disc is oval, obliquely oriented, with a temporal crescent and an intact rim; it is benign, often seen with high myopia, and must not be mistaken for glaucoma.
items.a: Tilted disc

items.c: Remember: Tilted disc is oblique and oval with inferonasal vessel displacement, is congenital, is often seen in myopia, and is usually benign.
items.a: Tilted disc

items.c: Remember: a conjunctival membrane covering the whole cornea with vessels indicates corneal conjunctivalization from limbal stem cell deficiency, a surgical emergency that threatens vision.
items.a: Case 6 (Slit_lamp): expert findings

items.c: Remember: CRVO shows venous engorgement and hemorrhages in all four quadrants (blood and thunder pattern), whereas BRVO involves a single quadrant and CRAO shows a pale retina with a cherry-red spot.
items.a: Case 11 (SLO): expert findings

items.c: Remember: a corrugated, elevated retina with a visible retinal break in a myope with photopsia and a shadow curtain is rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, a sight-threatening emergency requiring urgent repair.
items.a: Case 13 (SLO): expert findings

items.c: Remember: Triad of retinitis pigmentosa = night blindness, peripheral (concentric) field constriction and bone-spicule pigmentation, with arteriolar attenuation and waxy disc pallor; ERG shows reduced or absent rod responses.
items.a: Case 17 (SLO): expert findings

items.c: Remember: a full-thickness macular hole is a complete break from ILM to RPE at the fovea, classically caused by vitreofoveal traction and treated with vitrectomy, ILM peeling, and gas tamponade.
items.a: Case 31 (OCT): expert findings

items.c: Remember: drusen appear on OCT as undulating elevations of the hyperreflective RPE band with reduced reflectivity beneath, and AREDS2 supplementation is the established treatment for intermediate or advanced dry AMD.
items.a: Case 35 (OCT): expert findings

items.c: Remember: a normal macular OCT shows a preserved foveal depression with well-defined, evenly thick retinal layers and no intraretinal or subretinal fluid.
items.a: Normal (emmetropia)

items.c: Remember: diabetic macular edema on OCT shows intraretinal cystoid spaces and central subfield thickening; anti-VEGF is first-line when the fovea is involved.
items.a: Diabetic macular edema

items.c: Remember: epiretinal membrane shows a hyper-reflective surface band with retinal wrinkling on OCT, causing metamorphopsia, whereas a macular hole shows a full-thickness foveal break.
items.a: Epiretinal membrane

items.c: Remember: DME is the commonest cause of vision loss in DR, and OCT intraretinal cystoid spaces with central subfield thickening are the key imaging sign.
items.a: Diabetic macular edema

items.c: Remember: a healthy disc has a thick, uniform neuroretinal rim (ISNT rule: inferior is greater than superior is greater than nasal is greater than temporal) and a cup-to-disc ratio below 0.5 with no notching or splinter haemorrhage.
items.a: Healthy disc

items.c: Remember: a healthy disc has an intact, pink, uniformly thick neuroretinal rim (ISNT rule: inferior is thickest, then superior, nasal, temporal) with a small physiological cup.
items.a: Healthy disc

items.c: Remember: A healthy disc has a uniform, pink neuroretinal rim following the ISNT rule, a small symmetric cup, and a CDR below 0.3 with no notching or haemorrhage; any focal rim loss or disc haemorrhage should prompt glaucoma evaluation.
items.a: Healthy disc

items.c: Remember: a healthy disc has an intact ISNT rim, a small physiologic cup, and no notching or disc haemorrhage; always correlate the disc appearance with IOP, visual fields, and RNFL imaging before diagnosing glaucoma.
items.a: Healthy disc

items.c: Remember: a healthy disc has an ISNT-compliant rim (inferior is greater than superior is greater than nasal is greater than temporal), a cup-to-disc ratio under about 0.5, and symmetric discs between the two eyes.
items.a: Healthy disc

items.c: Remember: a healthy disc has an intact ISNT-patterned rim and a small, symmetric cup (cup-to-disc ratio below 0.5 with no asymmetry); diagnose glaucoma only with structural rim loss plus corresponding OCT or visual field defect.
items.a: Healthy disc

items.c: Remember: a healthy disc has a pink, intact neuroretinal rim following the ISNT rule, a small symmetric cup-to-disc ratio, and no notching, haemorrhage, or peripapillary atrophy.
items.a: Healthy disc

items.c: Remember: glaucomatous optic neuropathy shows an increased cup-to-disc ratio with rim thinning and notching, and the ISNT rule (inferior, superior, nasal, temporal rim thickness) is usually violated.
items.a: Glaucomatous disc

items.c: Remember: glaucomatous optic neuropathy is defined by structural loss of the neuroretinal rim and an enlarged cup, not by IOP alone.
items.a: Glaucomatous disc

items.c: Remember: glaucomatous optic neuropathy = large pale cup, thinned inferior and superior rim (ISNT rule), with the cup-to-disc ratio greater than 0.6 suggesting disease.
items.a: Glaucomatous disc

items.c: Remember: in glaucoma the cup enlarges and the neuroretinal rim thins, with vessels bending nasally at the disc edge; the disc is pale and excavated, not swollen.
items.a: Glaucomatous disc

items.c: Remember: a large, pale, excavated cup with bayoneting of vessels and asymmetry between eyes indicates glaucomatous optic neuropathy until proven otherwise.
items.a: Glaucomatous disc

items.c: Remember: No DR means zero microaneurysms, haemorrhages, exudates, cotton wool spots, venous beading, IRMA, or neovascularisation; long diabetes duration alone does not imply retinopathy.
items.a: No retinopathy

items.c: Remember: no diabetic retinopathy means a normal fundus with no microaneurysms, haemorrhages, exudates, IRMA, venous beading, or new vessels; a single microaneurysm alone upgrades the grade to mild NPDR.
items.a: No retinopathy

items.c: Remember: No DR means no microaneurysms, haemorrhages, exudates, or neovascularisation on fundus examination; screen again in 12 months for diabetics with no retinopathy.
items.a: No retinopathy

items.c: Remember: no DR means no microaneurysms, haemorrhages, exudates, cotton-wool spots, venous beading, IRMA, or neovascularisation on fundus photography; screen annually once the patient is well controlled.
items.a: No retinopathy

items.c: Remember: mild NPDR = microaneurysms only; add dot-blot haemorrhages for moderate; add cotton wool spots, venous beading, or IRMA for severe NPDR; new vessels define PDR.
items.a: Mild non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR)

items.c: Remember: Microaneurysms alone = mild NPDR; add haemorrhages, exudates or cotton wool spots in more than one quadrant = moderate NPDR; add IRMA, venous beading or neovascularisation = severe NPDR or PDR (4-2-1 rule).
items.a: Mild non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR)

items.c: Remember: mild NPDR = microaneurysms only; moderate adds haemorrhages, hard exudates or cotton wool spots; severe uses the 4-2-1 rule; PDR = neovascularisation or vitreous haemorrhage.
items.a: Mild non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR)

items.c: Remember the 4-2-1 rule: haemorrhages in all 4 quadrants, venous beading in 2 or more quadrants, or IRMA in 1 quadrant defines severe NPDR, with about 50 percent risk of PDR within 1 year.
items.a: Severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR)

items.c: Remember: neovascularisation at the disc (NVD) or elsewhere (NVE) = PDR; new vessels bleed easily, so sudden painless vision loss in a diabetic should prompt a search for vitreous haemorrhage and PRP.
items.a: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR)

items.c: Remember: Stage 1 is a flat line, Stage 2 a raised ridge, Stage 3 a ridge with extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation, and Stage 4 a partial detachment; Stage 3 with plus disease or zone I/II meets treatment thresholds.
items.a: Stage 3

items.c: Remember: Stage 1 is a line, stage 2 is a ridge, stage 3 is a ridge with extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation, stage 4 is partial detachment, and stage 5 is total detachment.
items.a: Stage 3

items.c: Remember: Stage 1 is a flat line, Stage 2 is a raised ridge, Stage 3 is a ridge with extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation, and Stage 4 is partial detachment; stage 3 is the key threshold for treatment in high-risk eyes.
items.a: Stage 3

items.c: Remember: Stage 1 is a flat line, stage 2 is an elevated ridge, stage 3 adds extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation, and stage 4 is partial detachment.
items.a: Stage 2

items.c: Remember: stage 1 is a flat line, stage 2 is a raised ridge, stage 3 is ridge with extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation, stage 4 is partial retinal detachment, and stage 5 is total retinal detachment.
items.a: Stage 2

items.c: Remember: ROP Stage 4 is partial detachment, Stage 5 is total funnel-shaped detachment (Stage 5 = Total, a funnel-shaped retinal fold behind the lens).
items.a: Stage 5

items.c: Remember: Aggressive posterior ROP (A-ROP) affects the posterior pole with no clear ridge, progresses rapidly within days, and needs urgent treatment.
items.a: Aggressive ROP (A-ROP)

items.c: Remember: A-ROP is posterior, rapidly progressive, lacks a clear demarcation ridge, and needs treatment within days of detection.
items.a: Aggressive ROP (A-ROP)

items.c: Remember: A-ROP is posterior-predominant, rapidly progressive, with plus disease and no classic staging ridge; treat urgently as it can progress to retinal detachment within days.
items.a: Aggressive ROP (A-ROP)

items.c: Remember: Stage 4 ROP = partial retinal detachment (4A extrafoveal, 4B foveal involvement); Stage 5 = total funnel detachment.
items.a: Stage 4

items.c: Remember: ROP stage 4 = partial retinal detachment (4A extrafoveal, 4B foveal); stage 5 = total detachment.
items.a: Stage 4

items.c: Remember: Stage 4 ROP = partial retinal detachment (4A extrafoveal, 4B foveal involvement); Stage 5 = total detachment.
items.a: Stage 4

items.c: Remember: a grey-white, atrophic, fibrotic macular lesion with preserved peripheral vision and a healthy disc points to a macular scar, the permanent end-stage of previous chorioretinal damage.
items.a: Macular scar

items.c: Remember: a macular scar is an irreversible, depigmented, fibrous area of chorioretinal atrophy; it is non-progressive, so check OCT and angiography for any active choroidal neovascular membrane before labelling it as inactive.
items.a: Macular scar

items.c: Remember: central serous chorioretinopathy is a young male, stress and steroid-associated, unilateral, self-limiting serous macular detachment; diagnose with OCT and fluorescein angiography (FA).
items.a: Central serous retinopathy

items.c: Remember: CSCR is a young male with stress or steroid use, a unilateral dome-shaped serous macular detachment on fundus, and most cases resolve within 3 months; confirm with OCT and FA/ICGA.
items.a: Central serous retinopathy

items.c: Remember: discrete yellow-white chorioretinal lesions with vitreous cells in a young patient suggest chorioretinitis, and toxoplasmosis is the commonest infectious cause.
items.a: Chorioretinitis

items.c: Remember: cupping means a large cup-to-disc ratio with a thin rim; papilledema means swollen, blurred disc margins.
items.a: Optic disc cupping

items.c: Remember: a sharply demarcated bright red patch on the bulbar conjunctiva with no pain, no discharge and normal vision is subconjunctival haemorrhage, which is usually benign and self-limiting, but check blood pressure and systemic risk factors.
items.a: Case 3 (Slit_lamp): expert findings

items.c: Remember: posterior synechiae, an irregular pupil, and cells and flare in the anterior chamber with ciliary flush point to anterior uveitis; check HLA-B27 and syphilis serology.
items.a: Case 9 (Slit_lamp): expert findings

items.c: Remember: A dense white lens opacity in an elderly patient is an advanced (white) age-related cataract; the lens is opaque enough to block the red reflex and fundus view, and phacoemulsification is the definitive treatment.
